trace.claim: The paper asks how substance use and individual characteristics shape friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools, a gap in existing research.
Peer ties in AI-majority reservation schools are organized by structural and demographic commonalities rather than by risky behaviors, challenging assumptions used in network-based prevention.
The study uses social network data from 9th and 10th graders in three Northern Plains reservation schools analyzed with ERGMs.
Reciprocity and transitivity are strong universal structural drivers of friendship in all three schools.
Substance use shows no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects on friendship formation.
trace.new_claim: Substance use shows no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily association with friendship formation.

trace.claim: Gender and grade homophily are primary axes of friendship formation across schools.
Depression and AI identity are substantively unrelated to friendship sending, receiving, or homophily.
The authors note the sample is limited to three schools on one reservation and is cross-sectional, so findings may not generalize.
The authors position the work as moving beyond generalizations from heterogeneous-school network literature to provide culturally grounded insights for AI adolescent social worlds.
Rees, Freng, and Winfree claim AI adolescents have fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers in heterogeneous school contexts, a descriptive finding the paper disputes in AI-majority settings.
